facts.text: 開発会社、デザイン会社、マーケティング代理店、フリーランス向けのプロジェクト管理ツール。タスク管理、時間記録、請求書、顧客に見せる専用画面、GitHub・GitLab連携をまとめている。コードのPRが開くとタスクが「レビュー」へ、マージされると「完了」へ動き、請求用に時刻を記録する。Asana・ClickUp・Linearからデータを取り込める。
無料プランは10ユーザーまで・プロジェクト無制限・250タスク・保存1GB。Plusは1ユーザー月6ドル（年払い、月払いは8ドル）。Pro Unlimitedはユーザー無制限で月99ドル（年払い、月払いは129ドル）、保存500GB。
紹介プログラムは、紹介した客1人ごとに生涯続く継続コミッションを払う。募集先はブログ運営者、比較サイト、インフルエンサー、既存の客。
創業者Pratham Naikは、SEO担当として複数の顧客案件を抱え、複雑な管理ツールにうんざりして作り始めたと書く。Asanaは簡単なタスクを作るだけで宇宙船の操縦のようで、Mondayは使わない機能にも払っており、Trelloは単純すぎたという。
2025年8月19日の本人投稿は、開始から6か月で稼働847チーム、MRR 4,200ドル（年末に10,000ドルが目標）、月の解約率8%、NPS 67と申告。新規登録の約4割は口コミ・紹介で、見た目と実際に使える無料枠が効き、顧客用の画面が最大の差になったと書く。

2025年11月3日の本人投稿は、インディー開発者仲間の要望（ダークモード、API、Notion風ブロック）で6か月作ったが、Product Huntは23票、初月売上は227ドルだったと書く。初めて話した代理店の経営者（インディー界隈の外の最初の客）に「顧客用ポータルは？白ラベルにできる？」と聞かれ、見た目より顧客とのやり取りの機能が要ると分かった。以後は事業主との直接の会話に切り替え、2か月で継続率が12%から41%、MRRが347ドルから2,100ドルになったという。
2025年9月30日の本人投稿は、3週間の聞き取りで「使いたい」という回答が200件超あり、6か月の毎日の公開開発を経ても、サインアップ43件・有料2件・MRR 18ドルだったと書く。以後は、不完全な解決策にすでに払っている人を探し、作る前に99ドルを先払いしてもよいという12人を見つけてから作り始めた。
2025年10月7日の本人投稿は、買い切り999ドル（ユーザーも案件も無制限）を、月額の選択肢と並べて4か月試した結果として、売上の約4割が買い切り、買い切りの客は月額の客の3.2倍を紹介、買い切り客の解約はゼロだが問い合わせは多いと書く。懸念として、サーバー費は利用に比例するので、買い切りの客が50人規模のチームを入れると利益が崩れると自分で書いている。

From Frustration to $4.2k MRR: The Teamcamp Project Management Story
by Pratham Naik
Hey IndieHackers! 👋
I'm sharing our journey building Teamcamp, a project management tool born out of pure frustration with bloated PM software.
The Problem That Started Everything
As an SEO executive managing multiple client projects, I was drowning in overly complex PM tools. Asana felt like piloting a spaceship just to create a simple task. Monday.com had so many features I never used but paid for. Trello was too basic for our needs.
The breaking point? My team spent more time managing the management tool than actually managing projects.
How Teamcamp Fixes This
We built Teamcamp around the principle of "All Together, All Aligned" - bringing projects, teams, and clients into one unified space without the complexity.
Core features that actually matter:
✅ Unified Project Dashboard - Real-time view of all projects and resources
✅ Milestone & Deadline Tracking - Never miss another deadline
✅ Task Prioritization - Smart priority management without overwhelming notifications
✅ Total Transparency - Keep clients in the loop automatically
✅ Seamless Collaboration - Team communication that doesn't feel like noise
Our Transparent Progress (6 months in)
Users: 847 active teams
MRR: $4,200 (target: $10k by end of year)
Churn: 8% monthly (industry avg: 12-15%)
NPS Score: 67 (we're proud of this!)
What's working:
Word-of-mouth referrals (40% of new signups)
Focus on aesthetic UI with top-tier functionality
Free tier that provides genuine value
What's challenging:
Balancing feature requests with our "simplicity first" philosophy
Educating users that fewer features can mean better productivity
Key Lessons Learned
"All in one" doesn't mean "everything in one" - We focused on essential features that teams actually use daily
Client transparency builds trust - Our client portal feature became our biggest differentiator
Beautiful UI isn't vanity - Teams are 3x more likely to adopt tools that look and feel premium

I Spent 6 Months Building for Indie Hackers. My First Real Customer Taught Me I Was Wrong.
by Pratham Naik
I launched my project management tool in May.
It had every feature indie hackers said they wanted: simple pricing, lifetime deals, dark mode, API access, and Notion-like blocks.
I got 23 upvotes on Product Hunt. Made $227 in the first month from other builders. Felt like I was onto something.
Then I talked to my first customer outside the indie sphere. She was a small marketing agency owner.
Within 5 minutes, she asked: "Where's the client portal? How do I white-label this? Can my clients comment without creating accounts?"
I had built none of those things.
I'd spent six months in indie hacker communities asking what features people wanted. Everyone said "Keep it simple! Don't bloat it!" So I built a tool that indie hackers loved to compliment but never actually paid for long-term.
The agency owner? She needed something that solved her actual pain: client communication chaos.
Not another "beautiful, minimal" tool.
I stopped posting feature polls on Twitter. Started booking 15-minute calls with people who fit my target customer profile but had never heard of indie hacking.
Real retention jumped from 12% to 41% in two months. MRR went from $347 to $2,100. Not huge numbers, but actual customers with real problems, not other founders window shopping.
The uncomfortable truth I learned: The indie hacker community is amazing for support and learning.
But it's a terrible place to validate most products. We are not representative of normal users. We want different things. We tolerate different friction.
My agency customer doesn't care about my tech stack. She doesn't want to "build in public" with me.
She just wants her clients to stop emailing her 47 times a day with feedback scattered across Gmail, Slack, and text messages.
When was the last time you talked to a potential customer who isn't an indie hacker or founder?
I'd love to hear your experiences. Have you caught yourself doing this? Or did you avoid this trap from the start? What helped you stay focused on real customer problems?

I validated my idea with almost 80+ people, built in public for 6 months, and still failed spectacularly
by Pratham Naik
Two years ago, I did everything "right" according to every indie hacker playbook.
Spent 3 weeks surveying potential users. Got 200+ responses saying "yes, I'd use this!" Posted daily updates on Twitter with #buildinpublic. Shared my journey on Reddit. Even got featured in a few newsletters.
6 months later: 43 total signups, 2 paying customers, $18 MRR.
The harsh truth nobody talks about:
Most indie hackers (including me) validate in echo chambers. We ask other builders, tweet to our founder followers, and get feedback from people who want to support us, not people who actually have the problem we're solving.
My biggest mistake: I validated the idea, not the business.
People said they'd use a "better project management tool." But when I built it, I realized they already had solutions they were happy enough with. Nobody was desperately searching for what I made.
What I learned the hard way:
Building in public is amazing for community and accountability. But it can create a false sense of validation. Other indie hackers cheering you on doesn't equal product-market fit.
The pivot that changed everything:
Instead of asking "would you use this?" I started asking "what did you pay for last month to solve this problem?" Completely different answers. Real money already being spent = real demand.
Now I validate differently:
Find people already paying for imperfect solutions
Test with strangers, not my network
Look for desperate searching behavior, not polite interest
Pre-sell before I build anything substantial
Using this approach, found 12 people willing to prepay $99 for a tool that doesn't exist yet. Only then did I start building.

Validating a "Lifetime Deal" Model for Project Management Software Am I Crazy?
by Pratham Naik
Testing a pricing hypothesis with Teamcamp that most SaaS experts say is financial suicide: $999 one-time payment for unlimited everything, forever.
The conventional wisdom:
Lifetime deals cannibalize recurring revenue. Customers expect perpetual support for zero ongoing income. You're leaving money on the table.
My contrarian bet:
Lifetime buyers become your most vocal advocates because they feel like they "beat the system". They have skin in the game, so they actually use the product instead of letting subscriptions ghost them.
Early validation data:
Launched 4 months ago with both $49/month and $999 lifetime options
40% of revenue comes from lifetime deals
Lifetime customers refer 3.2x more users than monthly subscribers
Support load is higher, but churn is obviously zero
The risks I am monitoring:
Server costs scale with usage, not revenue. If one lifetime customer brings on a 50-person team, my margins collapse. Feature requests from lifetime users feel more demanding because they paid upfront.
My validation question:
Has anyone here successfully run a lifetime deal model long-term? Did it work, or did it eventually break your business economics?
I am specifically worried about the 3-5 year horizon when early lifetime customers expect major feature updates.
Looking for honest experiences, not generic advice. If you tried lifetime pricing and it failed, I want to hear why.

facts.text: 開発会社、デザイン会社、マーケティング代理店、フリーランス向けのプロジェクト管理ツール。タスク管理、時間記録、請求書、顧客に見せる専用画面、GitHub・GitLab連携をまとめている。コードのPRが開くとタスクが「レビュー」へ、マージされると「完了」へ動き、請求用に時刻を記録する。Asana・ClickUp・Linearからデータを取り込める。
無料プランは10ユーザーまで・プロジェクト無制限・250タスク・保存1GB。Plusは1ユーザー月6ドル（年払い、月払いは8ドル）。Pro Unlimitedはユーザー無制限で月99ドル（年払い、月払いは129ドル）、保存500GB。
紹介プログラムは、紹介した客1人ごとに生涯続く継続コミッションを払う。募集先はブログ運営者、比較サイト、インフルエンサー、既存の客。
創業者Pratham Naikは、SEO担当として複数の顧客案件を抱え、複雑な管理ツールにうんざりして作り始めたと書く。Asanaは簡単なタスクを作るだけで宇宙船の操縦のようで、Mondayは使わない機能にも払っており、Trelloは単純すぎたという。
2025年8月19日の本人投稿は、開始から6か月で稼働847チーム、MRR 4,200ドル（年末に10,000ドルが目標）、月の解約率8%、NPS 67と申告。新規登録の約4割は口コミ・紹介で、見た目と実際に使える無料枠が効き、顧客用の画面が最大の差になったと書く。

2025年11月3日の本人投稿は、インディー開発者仲間の要望（ダークモード、API、Notion風ブロック）で6か月作ったが、Product Huntは23票、初月売上は227ドルだったと書く。初めて話した代理店の経営者（インディー界隈の外の最初の客）に「顧客用ポータルは？白ラベルにできる？」と聞かれ、見た目より顧客とのやり取りの機能が要ると分かった。以後は事業主との直接の会話に切り替え、2か月で継続率が12%から41%、MRRが347ドルから2,100ドルになったという。
2025年9月30日の本人投稿は、3週間の聞き取りで「使いたい」という回答が200件超あり、6か月の毎日の公開開発を経ても、サインアップ43件・有料2件・MRR 18ドルだったと書く。以後は、不完全な解決策にすでに払っている人を探し、作る前に99ドルを先払いしてもよいという12人を見つけてから作り始めた。
2025年10月7日の本人投稿は、買い切り999ドル（ユーザーも案件も無制限）を、月額の選択肢と並べて4か月試した結果として、売上の約4割が買い切り、買い切りの客は月額の客の3.2倍を紹介、買い切り客の解約はゼロだが問い合わせは多いと書く。懸念として、サーバー費は利用に比例するので、買い切りの客が50人規模のチームを入れると利益が崩れると自分で書いている。

From Frustration to $4.2k MRR: The Teamcamp Project Management Story
by Pratham Naik
Hey IndieHackers! 👋
I'm sharing our journey building Teamcamp, a project management tool born out of pure frustration with bloated PM software.
The Problem That Started Everything
As an SEO executive managing multiple client projects, I was drowning in overly complex PM tools. Asana felt like piloting a spaceship just to create a simple task. Monday.com had so many features I never used but paid for. Trello was too basic for our needs.
The breaking point? My team spent more time managing the management tool than actually managing projects.
How Teamcamp Fixes This
We built Teamcamp around the principle of "All Together, All Aligned" - bringing projects, teams, and clients into one unified space without the complexity.
Core features that actually matter:
✅ Unified Project Dashboard - Real-time view of all projects and resources
✅ Milestone & Deadline Tracking - Never miss another deadline
✅ Task Prioritization - Smart priority management without overwhelming notifications
✅ Total Transparency - Keep clients in the loop automatically
✅ Seamless Collaboration - Team communication that doesn't feel like noise
Our Transparent Progress (6 months in)
Users: 847 active teams
MRR: $4,200 (target: $10k by end of year)
Churn: 8% monthly (industry avg: 12-15%)
NPS Score: 67 (we're proud of this!)
What's working:
Word-of-mouth referrals (40% of new signups)
Focus on aesthetic UI with top-tier functionality
Free tier that provides genuine value
What's challenging:
Balancing feature requests with our "simplicity first" philosophy
Educating users that fewer features can mean better productivity
Key Lessons Learned
"All in one" doesn't mean "everything in one" - We focused on essential features that teams actually use daily
Client transparency builds trust - Our client portal feature became our biggest differentiator
Beautiful UI isn't vanity - Teams are 3x more likely to adopt tools that look and feel premium

I Spent 6 Months Building for Indie Hackers. My First Real Customer Taught Me I Was Wrong.
by Pratham Naik
I launched my project management tool in May.
It had every feature indie hackers said they wanted: simple pricing, lifetime deals, dark mode, API access, and Notion-like blocks.
I got 23 upvotes on Product Hunt. Made $227 in the first month from other builders. Felt like I was onto something.
Then I talked to my first customer outside the indie sphere. She was a small marketing agency owner.
Within 5 minutes, she asked: "Where's the client portal? How do I white-label this? Can my clients comment without creating accounts?"
I had built none of those things.
I'd spent six months in indie hacker communities asking what features people wanted. Everyone said "Keep it simple! Don't bloat it!" So I built a tool that indie hackers loved to compliment but never actually paid for long-term.
The agency owner? She needed something that solved her actual pain: client communication chaos.
Not another "beautiful, minimal" tool.
I stopped posting feature polls on Twitter. Started booking 15-minute calls with people who fit my target customer profile but had never heard of indie hacking.
Real retention jumped from 12% to 41% in two months. MRR went from $347 to $2,100. Not huge numbers, but actual customers with real problems, not other founders window shopping.
The uncomfortable truth I learned: The indie hacker community is amazing for support and learning.
But it's a terrible place to validate most products. We are not representative of normal users. We want different things. We tolerate different friction.
My agency customer doesn't care about my tech stack. She doesn't want to "build in public" with me.
She just wants her clients to stop emailing her 47 times a day with feedback scattered across Gmail, Slack, and text messages.
When was the last time you talked to a potential customer who isn't an indie hacker or founder?
I'd love to hear your experiences. Have you caught yourself doing this? Or did you avoid this trap from the start? What helped you stay focused on real customer problems?

I validated my idea with almost 80+ people, built in public for 6 months, and still failed spectacularly
by Pratham Naik
Two years ago, I did everything "right" according to every indie hacker playbook.
Spent 3 weeks surveying potential users. Got 200+ responses saying "yes, I'd use this!" Posted daily updates on Twitter with #buildinpublic. Shared my journey on Reddit. Even got featured in a few newsletters.
6 months later: 43 total signups, 2 paying customers, $18 MRR.
The harsh truth nobody talks about:
Most indie hackers (including me) validate in echo chambers. We ask other builders, tweet to our founder followers, and get feedback from people who want to support us, not people who actually have the problem we're solving.
My biggest mistake: I validated the idea, not the business.
People said they'd use a "better project management tool." But when I built it, I realized they already had solutions they were happy enough with. Nobody was desperately searching for what I made.
What I learned the hard way:
Building in public is amazing for community and accountability. But it can create a false sense of validation. Other indie hackers cheering you on doesn't equal product-market fit.
The pivot that changed everything:
Instead of asking "would you use this?" I started asking "what did you pay for last month to solve this problem?" Completely different answers. Real money already being spent = real demand.
Now I validate differently:
Find people already paying for imperfect solutions
Test with strangers, not my network
Look for desperate searching behavior, not polite interest
Pre-sell before I build anything substantial
Using this approach, found 12 people willing to prepay $99 for a tool that doesn't exist yet. Only then did I start building.

Server costs scale with usage, not revenue. If one lifetime customer brings on a 50-person team, my margins collapse. Feature requests from lifetime users feel more demanding because they paid upfront.
